## Choose **one** prompt to answer

> **Prompt A:** `r params$p1`

## Response

<!-- RESPONSE-START -->
There is no need to put quotes around the word leap. The very act of calling it a leap signals that something uncertain lies beneath. An inference is merely a selection of thoughts made from a larger population of possibilities. Underline possibilities. Making an inference of a sample of ideas, built out to a pattern that seems meaningful vacillates between what is observed and what may still be hidden. An inference or leap doesn’t always have a safe, sound landing spot.
Looking for and potentially finding a pattern in a sample of research must be exciting. It suggests that the world beyond the sample resembles what is seen to bear out in the inference. However, it is not enough to find a pattern, because samples are noisy, messy, and vulnerable to chance. A small sample might show a strong difference where none exists. A biased sample selection might show a trend that reflects nothing except the method of what you’re selecting to look at. Just as words can sound or be read as more authoritative than they deserve, sample size patterns can appear more meaningful than they really are.
In a sort of research antidote, hypothesis testing offers a kind of gentle intellectual smack across the face, interrupting the instinct to generalize too quickly. The hypothesis that doesn’t work out becomes a counterweight to the pull of the observed pattern. In this way, hypothesis testing creates skepticism. Sticking to your hypotheses can help weather the storm of jumping to inferences. Asking yourself, “Is this what I thought was going to happen?” may be just enough to see the broader research landscape.
However, the allure of making an inference/leap remains and so do the risks that come with leaping to conclusions. A statistically significant result does not guarantee that its impact is large or practically important. It does not guarantee that conditions were met, that data was collected without bias, or that I resisted the temptation to test so many hypotheses until one appeared significant. Statistically significant findings can give an illusion of certainty, just as me writing this journal prompt to 500 words can give an illusion of completeness or truth to what I’m typing.
An inference does not escape uncertainty because it is built from incomplete information. A sample is only a small measure of a population. Even a statistically significant point retains a bit of doubt, like the recognition that chance still shapes the world in every hour of our lives. Acknowledging uncertainty does not weaken inference. It does place it on honest ground.
An inference in research findings becomes trustworthy not because it eliminates risk, but because it manages it. Intentional survey design and careful interpretation of the data found in the research strengthens the “leap”. It offers understanding while acknowledging the limits that define the act of inferring itself.
<!-- RESPONSE-END -->

## Word Count & Range Check

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
get_response_text <- function() {
  f <- knitr::current_input()
  if (is.null(f) || !file.exists(f)) return("")
  x <- readLines(f, warn = FALSE)
  # Find the lines that EXACTLY match the start/end markers
  s <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-START -->$", x)
  e <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-END -->$", x)
  if (length(s) != 1 || length(e) != 1 || e <= s) return("")
  paste(x[(s + 1L):(e - 1L)], collapse = "\n")
}
count_words <- function(txt) {
  # Remove code blocks and inline code before counting
  txt <- gsub("```[\\s\\S]*?```", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- gsub("`[^`]*`", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Keep letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens, and apostrophes
  txt <- gsub("[^\\p{L}\\p{N}\\s'-]", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Split by whitespace and count non-empty words
  words <- unlist(strsplit(txt, "\\s+", perl = TRUE))
  words <- words[nzchar(words)]
  length(words)
}
txt <- get_response_text()
n <- count_words(txt)
minw <- as.integer(params$word_min)
maxw <- as.integer(params$word_max)
in_range <- n >= minw && n <= maxw
cat(sprintf("**Word count:** %d  \n", n))
cat(sprintf("**Required range (%s):** %d–%d words  \n",
            toupper(params$course), minw, maxw))
cat(if (in_range) "**Status:** ✅ In range\n" else "**Status:** ❌ Out of range\n")
```
